audioscript.text: Louise Taylor.

audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: No, I'm actually Canadian, though my mother was British.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: And your date of birth?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: December 14th, 1977.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: So you're just visiting this country?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I come over most summers on business.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I'm an interior designer, and I come over to buy old furniture, antiques you know.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: There are some really lovely things around here.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: But you need to get out to the small towns.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I've had a really good trip this year, until this happened.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: OK, so you've been here quite a while?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I'm here for 2 months, I go back next week.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: So, may I ask where you're staying now?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Well, at present, I've got a place at Park Apartments, that's on King Street.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I was staying at the Riverside Apartments on the same street, but the apartment there was only available for six weeks, so I had to find another one.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: OK. And the apartment Number?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Fifteen.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Now, I need to take some details of the theft.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: So, you said you had some things stolen out of your bag.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: And were you actually carrying the bag when the theft took place?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I really can't understand it.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I had my backpack on, and I went into a supermarket to buy a few things, and when I opened it up, my wallet wasn't there.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: And what did your wallet have in it?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Well, fortunately, I don't keep my credit cards in that wallet.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: I keep them with my passport in an inside compartment in my backpack.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: But there was quite a bit of cash there, about £250 Sterling I should think.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE
audioscript.explain: Q4: Louise says there was *'about £250 Sterling'* in the wallet. She withdrew £300 but spent about £50, so the amount stolen was **250**. The answer is **250**.

audioscript.text: I withdrew £300 from my account yesterday.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE
audioscript.explain: Q4: Louise says there was *'about £250 Sterling'* in the wallet. She withdrew £300 but spent about £50, so the amount stolen was **250**. The answer is **250**.

audioscript.text: But I did a bit of shopping, so I must have already spent about £50 of that.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE
audioscript.explain: Q4: Louise says there was *'about £250 Sterling'* in the wallet. She withdrew £300 but spent about £50, so the amount stolen was **250**. The answer is **250**.

audioscript.text: OK.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: At first I thought, oh, I must have left the wallet back in the apartment.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: But then I realized my phone had gone as well.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE
audioscript.explain: Q5: Louise says *'I realized my phone had gone as well'*. The question lists items stolen: a wallet and a ... So the second stolen item is a **phone**.

audioscript.text: It was only a week old, and that's when I realized I'd been robbed.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Anyway, at least they didn't take the keys to my rental car.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: So you say the theft occurred yesterday?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Yes.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: So that was September the 10th, and do you have any idea at all of where or when the things might possibly have been stolen?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER
audioscript.explain: Q6: The officer confirms the theft was yesterday, which was *'September the 10th'*. The question asks for the date of theft, so the answer is **10 September**.

audioscript.text: Well, at first I couldn't believe it, because the bag had been on my back ever since I left the apartment after lunch.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: It's just a small backpack.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: But I generally use it when I'm traveling, because it seems safer than a handbag.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Anyway, I met up with a friend, and we spent a couple of hours in the museum.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: But I do remember that as we were leaving there, at about 4 o'clock, a group of young boys ran up to us, and they were really crowding round us.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: And they were asking us what time it was, then all of a sudden, they ran off.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE
audioscript.explain: Q8: Louise says the boys *'were asking us what time it was'*. The question says some boys asked for the ... then ran off. So they asked for the **time**.

audioscript.text: Can you remember anything about them?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: The one who did most of the talking.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Was wearing a T-shirt with a picture of something.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Ah. Let's see, a tiger.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Right, any idea of how old he might have been?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Around 12 years old.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: And can you remember anything else about his appearance?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Not much, he was quite thin.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Color of hair?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: I do remember that, he was blonde.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE
audioscript.explain: Q9: Louise describes the main boy: *'he was blonde'*. The question asks for his hair color, so the answer is **blonde**.

audioscript.text: All the others were dark haired.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: And any details of the others?
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: Not really.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: They came and went so quickly.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: So what I'm going to do now is give you a crime reference number, so you can contact your insurance company.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER

audioscript.text: So, this is 10 digits, 8795482361.
audioscript.speaker: OFFICER
audioscript.explain: Q10: The officer gives the crime reference number: *'8795482361'*. The question asks for this number, so the answer is **8795482361**.

audioscript.text: Thank you.
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: So, should I contact the...
audioscript.speaker: LOUISE

audioscript.text: That is the end of section 1.

audioscript.text: Section 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a manager giving a welcome talk to a group of apprentices who are starting their training at the company.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning everyone.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: My name's Janet Parker, and I'm the Human Resources manager.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: We're very happy to welcome you to your new apprenticeship.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: I hope that the next 6 months will be a positive and enjoyable experience for you.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: I'd like to start with some general advice about being an apprentice.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: Most of you have very little or no experience of working for a big organization, and the first week or so may be quite challenging.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: There will be a lot of new information to take in, but don't worry too much about trying to remember everything.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: The important thing is to check with someone if you're not sure what to do.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER
audioscript.explain:
Q11: The manager says *'make an effort to talk to as many people as possible about their work'* — **'talk to as many people'** means **'get to know colleagues'**. So the answer is **A**.

Q12: The manager says *'check with someone if you're not sure what to do'* — **'check with someone'** means **'ask lots of questions'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: You'll find your supervisor is very approachable, and won't mind explaining things or helping you out.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: You're here to learn, so make the most of that opportunity.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: You'll be spending time in different departments during your first week, so make an effort to talk to as many people as possible about their work.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER
audioscript.explain:
Q11: The manager says *'make an effort to talk to as many people as possible about their work'* — **'talk to as many people'** means **'get to know colleagues'**. So the answer is **A**.

Q12: The manager says *'check with someone if you're not sure what to do'* — **'check with someone'** means **'ask lots of questions'**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: You'll make some new friends and find out lots of useful information.
audioscript.speaker: JANET PARKER

audioscript.text: As well as having a supervisor, you'll each be assigned a mentor.

audioscript.text: Burning fossil fuels like gas, coal and oil, seriously damages the environment, and they'll eventually run out.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For a number of years now, scientists have been working out how we can derive energy from renewable sources such as the sun and wind.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Today, I'll outline marine renewable energy, also called ocean energy, which harnesses the movement of the oceans.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Marine renewable energy can be divided into three main categories, wave energy, tidal energy, and ocean thermal energy conversion.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And I'll say a few words about each one.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: First, wave energy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Numerous devices have been invented to harvest wave energy with names such as Wave Dragon.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Penguin and Mighty Whale, and research is going on to try and come up with a really efficient method.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This form of energy has plenty of potential.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As the source is constant, and there's no danger of waves coming to a standstill.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says *'the source is constant'* — **'constant'** means it never stops. The question asks for an advantage: waves provide a **constant** source. So the answer is **constant**.

audioscript.text: Electricity can be generated using onshore systems, using a reservoir or offshore systems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But the problem with ocean waves is that they're erratic, with the wind making them travel in every direction.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says waves are *'erratic, with the wind making them travel in every direction'*. The question asks for a problem: waves can move in any **direction**. So the answer is **direction**.

audioscript.text: This adds to the difficulty of creating efficient technology.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ideally, all the waves would travel smoothly and regularly along the same straight line.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'sand and other sediment on the ocean floor'* might be stopped. The question asks where this movement happens — on the **floor** of the ocean. So the answer is **floor**.

audioscript.text: The second category of marine energy that I'll mention is tidal energy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One major advantage of using the tide, rather than waves as a source of energy is that it's predictable.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says one major advantage of tides over waves is that *'it's predictable'*. The question says tides are more **predictable** than waves. So the answer is **predictable**.

audioscript.text: We know the exact times of high and low tides for years to come.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For tidal energy to be effective, the difference between high and low tides needs to be at least 5 meters, and this occurs naturally in only about 40 places on earth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But the right conditions can be created by constructing a tidal lagoon, an area of seawater, separated from the sea.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One current plan is to create a tidal lagoon on the coast of Wales.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This will be an area of water within a bay at Swansea.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says the tidal lagoon will be *'an area of water within a bay at Swansea'*. The question asks where it will be created — in a **bay**. So the answer is **bay**.

audioscript.text: Sheltered by a U-shaped breakwater or dam built out from the coast, the breakwater will contain 16 hydro turbines.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And as the tide rises, water rushes through the breakwater, activating the turbines, which turn a generator to produce electricity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then, for three hours as the tide goes out, the water is held back within the breakwater, increasing the difference in water level until it's several meters higher within the lagoon, than in the open sea.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Then, in order to release the stored water, gates in the breakwater are opened, it pours powerfully out of the lagoon,

audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says *'gates in the breakwater are opened'* to release stored water. The question asks what the water is released through — **gates**. So the answer is **gates**.

audioscript.text: driving the turbines in the breakwater in the opposite direction, and again generating thousands of megawatts of electricity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As there are two high tides a day, this lagoon scheme would generate electricity four times a day, every day, for a total of around 14 hours in every 24.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And enough electricity for over 150,000 homes.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This system has quite a lot in its favor, unlike solar and wind energy, it doesn't depend on the weather.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The turbines are operated without the need for fuel.

audioscript.text: It's estimated that electricity generated in this way will be relatively cheap, and that manufacturing the components would create more than 2,000 jobs, a big boost to the local economy.

audioscript.text: On the other hand, there are fears that lagoons might harm both fish and birds, for example by disturbing migration patterns.

audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says lagoons might harm fish and birds by *'disturbing migration patterns'*. The question asks what is affected — **migration**. So the answer is **migration**.

audioscript.text: And causing a buildup of silt, affecting local ecosystems.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: There are other forms of tidal energy, but I'll go on to the third category of marine energy: ocean thermal energy conversion.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This depends on there being a big difference in temperature between surface water and the water a couple of kilometers below the surface, and this occurs in tropical coastal areas.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The idea is to bring cold water up to the surface using a submerged pipe.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear two environmental science students called Rosie and Martin discussing their presentation on an extinct animal called the woolly Mammoth with their tutor.

audioscript.text: OK, we've got a short outline here.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: Thanks, uh, so, it's about a research project in North America.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Yes, but we thought we needed something general about woolly mammoths in our introduction.
audioscript.speaker: MARTIN

audioscript.text: To establish that they were related to our modern elephant, and they lived thousands of years ago in the last ice age.
audioscript.speaker: MARTIN

audioscript.text: Maybe we could show a video clip of a cartoon about mammoths.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: But that would be a bit childish. Or we could have a diagram, it could be a timeline to show when they lived, with illustrations?
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: Then you're describing the discovery of the mammoth tooth on St Paul's Island in Alaska.
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: And why it was significant?
audioscript.speaker: TUTOR

audioscript.text: Yes, the tooth was found by a man called Russell Graham.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: He picked it up from under a rock in a cave.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: He knew it was special.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: For a start, it was in really good condition, as if it had been just extracted from the animal's jawbone.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: Anyway, they found it was 6,500 years old.
audioscript.speaker: ROSIE

audioscript.text: So why was that significant?

audioscript.text: In this series of lectures about the history of weather forecasting, I'll start by examining its early history.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That'll be the subject of today's talk.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: OK, so we'll start by going back thousands of years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Most ancient cultures had weather gods, and weather catastrophes such as floods, played an important role in many creation myths.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Generally, weather was attributed to the whims of the gods, as the wide range of weather gods in various cultures shows.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For instance, there's the Egyptian sun god Ra, and Thor, the Norse god of thunder and lightning.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Many ancient civilizations developed rites such as dances,
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says ancient civilizations developed *'rites such as dances'* to make weather gods kind — **'rites'** means **'ceremonies'**. So the answer is **dances**.

audioscript.text: in order to make the weather gods look kindly on them.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says ancient civilizations developed *'rites such as dances'* to make weather gods kind — **'rites'** means **'ceremonies'**. So the answer is **dances**.

audioscript.text: But the weather was of daily importance.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Observing the skies and drawing the correct conclusions from these observations was really important.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says observing the sky was important because *'their survival depended on it'* — **'survival'** is what they needed to ensure. So the answer is **survival**.

audioscript.text: In fact, their survival depended on it.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says observing the sky was important because *'their survival depended on it'* — **'survival'** is what they needed to ensure. So the answer is **survival**.

audioscript.text: It isn't known when people first started to observe the skies, but at around 650 BC, the Babylonians produced the first short range weather forecasts.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says Babylonians made forecasts *'based on their observations of clouds'* — **'clouds'** are the weather phenomena they used. So the answer is **clouds**.

audioscript.text: Based on their observations of clouds and other phenomena.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says Babylonians made forecasts *'based on their observations of clouds'* — **'clouds'** are the weather phenomena they used. So the answer is **clouds**.

audioscript.text: The Chinese also recognized weather patterns, and by 300 BC, astronomers had developed a calendar, which divided the year into 24 festivals.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says the Chinese calendar *'divided the year into 24 festivals'*, each linked to a weather phenomenon — **'festivals'** are the parts of the calendar. So the answer is **festivals**.

audioscript.text: Each associated with a different weather phenomenon.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says the Chinese calendar *'divided the year into 24 festivals'*, each linked to a weather phenomenon — **'festivals'** are the parts of the calendar. So the answer is **festivals**.

audioscript.text: The ancient Greeks were the first to develop a more scientific approach to explaining the weather.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The work of the philosopher and scientist Aristotle in the fourth century BC is especially noteworthy.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As his ideas held sway for nearly 2,000 years.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 340 BC, he wrote a book in which he attempted to account for the formation of rain, clouds, wind, and storms.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He also described celestial phenomena such as haloes - that is, bright circles of light around the sun, the moon, and bright stars - and comets.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says Aristotle described *'haloes ... and comets'* — **'comets'** are the second celestial phenomenon he mentioned. So the answer is **comets**.

audioscript.text: Many of his observations were surprisingly accurate.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For example, he believed that heat could cause water to evaporate.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: But he also jumped to quite a few wrong conclusions, such as that winds are breathed out by the earth.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Errors like this were rectified from the Renaissance onwards.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For nearly 2,000 years, Aristotle's work was accepted as the chief authority on weather theory.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Alongside this, though, in the Middle Ages, weather observations were passed on in the form of proverbs, such as "Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning".
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage gives a proverb about *'Red sky at night'* — the proverb's meaning depends on the colour of the **sky**. So the answer is **sky**.

audioscript.text: Many of these are based on very good observations, and are accurate, as contemporary meteorologists have discovered.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: For centuries, any attempt to forecast the weather could only be based on personal observations, but in the 15th century, scientists began to see the need for instruments. Until then, the only ones available were weather vanes to determine the wind direction.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says in the 15th century, scientists *'began to see the need for instruments'* — they recognized the value of **instruments** for the first time. So the answer is **instruments**.

audioscript.text: And early versions of rain gauges.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: One of the first invented in the 15th century was a hygrometer, which measured humidity.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This was one of many inventions that contributed to the development of weather forecasting.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 1592, the Italian scientist and inventor Galileo developed the world's first thermometer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says *'Galileo developed the world's first thermometer'* — he invented the **thermometer**. So the answer is **thermometer**.

audioscript.text: His student Torricelli later invented the barometer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Which allowed people to measure atmospheric pressure.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In 1648, the French philosopher Pascal proved that pressure decreases with altitude.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This discovery was verified by English astronomer Halley in 1686.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And Halley was also the first person to map trade winds.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This increasing ability to measure factors related to weather helped scientists to understand the atmosphere and its processes better, and they started collecting weather observation data systematically.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: In the 18th century, the scientist and politician Benjamin Franklin carried out work on electricity and lightning in particular, but he was also very interested in weather.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And studied it throughout most of his life.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was Franklin who discovered that storms generally travel from west to east.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says Franklin discovered that *'storms generally travel from west to east'* — he identified the movement of **storms**. So the answer is **storms**.

audioscript.text: In addition to new meteorological instruments, other developments contributed to our understanding of the atmosphere.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: People in different locations began to keep records.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And in the mid 19th century, the invention of the telegraph made it possible for these records to be collated.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says the *'invention of the telegraph'* allowed records from different places to be collated — **'collated'** means sent to the same place. So the answer is **telegraph**.

audioscript.text: This led by the end of the 19th century to the first weather services.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It was not until the early 20th century that mathematics and physics became part of meteorology, and we'll continue from that point next week.

utterances.text: In this series of lectures about the history of weather forecasting, I'll start by examining its early history.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: That'll be the subject of today's talk.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: OK, so we'll start by going back thousands of years.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Most ancient cultures had weather gods, and weather catastrophes such as floods, played an important role in many creation myths.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Generally, weather was attributed to the whims of the gods, as the wide range of weather gods in various cultures shows.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: For instance, there's the Egyptian sun god Ra, and Thor, the Norse god of thunder and lightning.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Many ancient civilizations developed rites such as dances,
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q31: The passage says ancient civilizations developed *'rites such as dances'* to make weather gods kind — **'rites'** means **'ceremonies'**. So the answer is **dances**.

utterances.text: in order to make the weather gods look kindly on them.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q31: The passage says ancient civilizations developed *'rites such as dances'* to make weather gods kind — **'rites'** means **'ceremonies'**. So the answer is **dances**.

utterances.text: But the weather was of daily importance.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Observing the skies and drawing the correct conclusions from these observations was really important.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q32: The passage says observing the sky was important because *'their survival depended on it'* — **'survival'** is what they needed to ensure. So the answer is **survival**.

utterances.text: In fact, their survival depended on it.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q32: The passage says observing the sky was important because *'their survival depended on it'* — **'survival'** is what they needed to ensure. So the answer is **survival**.

utterances.text: It isn't known when people first started to observe the skies, but at around 650 BC, the Babylonians produced the first short range weather forecasts.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q33: The passage says Babylonians made forecasts *'based on their observations of clouds'* — **'clouds'** are the weather phenomena they used. So the answer is **clouds**.

utterances.text: Based on their observations of clouds and other phenomena.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q33: The passage says Babylonians made forecasts *'based on their observations of clouds'* — **'clouds'** are the weather phenomena they used. So the answer is **clouds**.

utterances.text: The Chinese also recognized weather patterns, and by 300 BC, astronomers had developed a calendar, which divided the year into 24 festivals.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q34: The passage says the Chinese calendar *'divided the year into 24 festivals'*, each linked to a weather phenomenon — **'festivals'** are the parts of the calendar. So the answer is **festivals**.

utterances.text: Each associated with a different weather phenomenon.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q34: The passage says the Chinese calendar *'divided the year into 24 festivals'*, each linked to a weather phenomenon — **'festivals'** are the parts of the calendar. So the answer is **festivals**.

utterances.text: The ancient Greeks were the first to develop a more scientific approach to explaining the weather.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The work of the philosopher and scientist Aristotle in the fourth century BC is especially noteworthy.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: As his ideas held sway for nearly 2,000 years.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: In 340 BC, he wrote a book in which he attempted to account for the formation of rain, clouds, wind, and storms.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: He also described celestial phenomena such as haloes - that is, bright circles of light around the sun, the moon, and bright stars - and comets.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q35: The passage says Aristotle described *'haloes ... and comets'* — **'comets'** are the second celestial phenomenon he mentioned. So the answer is **comets**.

utterances.text: Many of his observations were surprisingly accurate.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: For example, he believed that heat could cause water to evaporate.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: But he also jumped to quite a few wrong conclusions, such as that winds are breathed out by the earth.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Errors like this were rectified from the Renaissance onwards.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: For nearly 2,000 years, Aristotle's work was accepted as the chief authority on weather theory.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Alongside this, though, in the Middle Ages, weather observations were passed on in the form of proverbs, such as "Red sky at night, shepherd's delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd's warning".
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q36: The passage gives a proverb about *'Red sky at night'* — the proverb's meaning depends on the colour of the **sky**. So the answer is **sky**.

utterances.text: Many of these are based on very good observations, and are accurate, as contemporary meteorologists have discovered.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: For centuries, any attempt to forecast the weather could only be based on personal observations, but in the 15th century, scientists began to see the need for instruments. Until then, the only ones available were weather vanes to determine the wind direction.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q37: The passage says in the 15th century, scientists *'began to see the need for instruments'* — they recognized the value of **instruments** for the first time. So the answer is **instruments**.

utterances.text: And early versions of rain gauges.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: One of the first invented in the 15th century was a hygrometer, which measured humidity.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This was one of many inventions that contributed to the development of weather forecasting.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: In 1592, the Italian scientist and inventor Galileo developed the world's first thermometer.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q38: The passage says *'Galileo developed the world's first thermometer'* — he invented the **thermometer**. So the answer is **thermometer**.

utterances.text: His student Torricelli later invented the barometer.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Which allowed people to measure atmospheric pressure.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: In 1648, the French philosopher Pascal proved that pressure decreases with altitude.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This discovery was verified by English astronomer Halley in 1686.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And Halley was also the first person to map trade winds.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This increasing ability to measure factors related to weather helped scientists to understand the atmosphere and its processes better, and they started collecting weather observation data systematically.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: In the 18th century, the scientist and politician Benjamin Franklin carried out work on electricity and lightning in particular, but he was also very interested in weather.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And studied it throughout most of his life.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It was Franklin who discovered that storms generally travel from west to east.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q39: The passage says Franklin discovered that *'storms generally travel from west to east'* — he identified the movement of **storms**. So the answer is **storms**.

utterances.text: In addition to new meteorological instruments, other developments contributed to our understanding of the atmosphere.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: People in different locations began to keep records.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And in the mid 19th century, the invention of the telegraph made it possible for these records to be collated.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q40: The passage says the *'invention of the telegraph'* allowed records from different places to be collated — **'collated'** means sent to the same place. So the answer is **telegraph**.

utterances.text: This led by the end of the 19th century to the first weather services.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It was not until the early 20th century that mathematics and physics became part of meteorology, and we'll continue from that point next week.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Section 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman talking to a group of college students about volunteering to help other people.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.

audioscript.text: Good morning, my name's Lucy Crittenden, and I'm the director of operations for an organization that arranges volunteering in this part of the country.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: I'm hoping I can persuade one or two of you to become volunteers yourselves.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Let me start by briefly explaining what we mean by volunteering.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Volunteers are teenagers and adults who choose to spend some time unpaid, helping other people in some way.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Most volunteers devote two or three hours to this every week.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: While a few do much more, the people they help may have physical or behavioral difficulties, for example. Volunteers can do all sorts of things, depending on their own abilities and interests.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: If they're supporting a family that's struggling for example, they may be able to give them tips on cooking.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Or recommend how to plan their budget, or how to shop sensibly on their income.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: They might even do some painting or wallpapering, perhaps alongside any members of the family.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

Q12: The passage says volunteers *'might even do some painting or wallpapering'* — **'painting or wallpapering'** means **'decorating'**. It also says they *'do some babysitting'* — **'babysitting'** is a form of **'childcare'**. So the two activities are **decorating** and **childcare**.

audioscript.text: Who are able to do it, or even do some babysitting, so that parents can go out for a while.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain:
Q11: The passage says volunteers *'might even do some painting or wallpapering'* — **'painting or wallpapering'** means **'decorating'**. It also says they *'do some babysitting'* — **'babysitting'** is a form of **'childcare'**. So the two activities are **decorating** and **childcare**.

Q12: The passage says volunteers *'might even do some painting or wallpapering'* — **'painting or wallpapering'** means **'decorating'**. It also says they *'do some babysitting'* — **'babysitting'** is a form of **'childcare'**. So the two activities are **decorating** and **childcare**.

audioscript.text: The benefit from volunteering isn't only for the people being helped, volunteers also gain from it.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: They're using their skills to cope with somebody's mental or physical ill health.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: And volunteering may be a valuable element of their CV when they're applying for jobs.

So the two benefits are **having a sense of purpose** and **boosting their employment prospects**.

audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Significantly, most volunteers feel that what they're doing gives them a purpose in their lives, and in my opinion, they're lucky in that respect.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain:

audioscript.text: As many people don't have that feeling.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now, I'd like to tell you what some of our volunteers have said about what they do, to give you an idea of the range of ways in which they can help people.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Habib supports an elderly lady who's beginning to show signs of dementia.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Once a week, they along with other elderly people, go to the local community center, where a group of people come in and sing.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: The songs take the listeners back to their youth.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says for Habib, *'the songs take the listeners back to their youth'* — **'back to their youth'** means they **'remember past times'**. So the answer is **F**.

audioscript.text: And for a little while, they can forget the difficulties that they face now.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Our volunteer Consuela is an amazing woman.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: She has difficulty walking herself.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: But she doesn't let that stop her.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: She helps a couple of people with similar difficulties, who had almost stopped walking altogether, by using herself as an example.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain: Q16: The passage says Consuela helps people *'who had almost stopped walking altogether'* — **'almost stopped walking'** is a **physical difficulty**. She helps them **'overcome'** it by encouraging them to walk more. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: Consuela encourages them to walk more and more.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Minh visits a young man who lives alone, and can't leave his home on his own.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: So he hardly ever saw anyone, but together they go out to the cinema.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain: Q17: The passage says Minh visits a man who *'hardly ever saw anyone'* — this means he was **isolated**. But together they *'go out to the cinema'* — this helps him **'escape isolation'**. So the answer is **E**.

audioscript.text: Or to see friends, the young man hadn't been able to visit for a long time.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Tanya visits an elderly woman once a week.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: When the woman found out that Tanya is a professional dressmaker.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: She got interested.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Tanya showed her some soft toys she'd made, and the woman decided to try it herself.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain: Q18: The passage says Tanya showed the woman *'soft toys she'd made, and the woman decided to try it herself'* — **'decided to try it herself'** means she **'started a new hobby'**. So the answer is **G**.

audioscript.text: And now she really enjoys it, and spends hours making toys.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: They're not perhaps up to Tanya's standard yet, but she gains a lot of pleasure from doing it.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Alexei is a volunteer with a family that faces a number of difficulties.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: By calmly talking over possible solutions with family members, he's helping them to realize that they aren't helpless, and that they can do something themselves to improve their situation.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain: Q19: The passage says Alexei helps the family realize *'they can do something themselves to improve their situation'* — **'do something themselves'** means they **'solve problems independently'**. So the answer is **D**.

audioscript.text: This has been great for their self-esteem, and the last volunteer I'll mention, though there are plenty more, is Juba.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: She volunteers with a teenage girl with learning difficulties.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Who wasn't very good at talking to other people.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Juba's worked very patiently with her, and now the girl is far better at expressing herself, and at understanding other people.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN
audioscript.explain: Q20: The passage says Juba helped the girl become *'far better at expressing herself, and at understanding other people'* — **'expressing herself'** and **'understanding other people'** are **communication skills**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: OK, I hope that's given you an idea of what volunteering is all about.
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: Now I'd like to talk to you about...
audioscript.speaker: LUCY CRITTENDEN

audioscript.text: That is the end of section 2.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

audioscript.text: Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a British university lecturer in music talking about concerts in an arts festival.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: As you all know, the university is planning an arts festival for later this year, and here in the music department, we've planned three concerts.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: These will be public performances, and the program has just been finalized.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The theme of the festival is links between the UK and Australia.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And this is reflected in the music.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Each concert will feature both British and Australian composers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: I'll tell you briefly about the Australian music.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As you probably won't be familiar with that.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The first concert will include music by Liza Lim, who was born in Perth, Western Australia in 1966.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As a child Lim originally learned to play the piano like so many children, and also the violin.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q31: The passage says Lim *'learned to play the piano... and also the violin'* — the question asks what she studied besides piano. So the answer is **violin**.

audioscript.text: But when she was 11, her teachers encouraged her to start composing.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: She found this was her real strength, and she studied and later taught composition, both in Australia and in other countries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: As a composer, she has received commissions from numerous orchestras, other performers, and festivals in several countries.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Liza Lim's compositions are vibrant and full of energy, and she often explores Asian and Australian Aboriginal cultural sources.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q32: The passage says her compositions are *'vibrant and full of energy'* — **'full of'** means they show a great deal of it. So the answer is **energy**.

audioscript.text: Including the native instrument the didgeridoo.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is featured in a work called The Compass.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Her music is very expressive.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: So although it is complex, it has the power of connecting with audiences and performers alike.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q33: The passage says *'although it is complex, it has the power of connecting'* — the question says her music is expressive and also something. So the answer is **complex**.

audioscript.text: In the festival, we're going to give a semi-staged performance of The Oresteia.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: This is an opera in seven parts, based on the trilogy of ancient Greek tragedies.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q34: The passage says *'This is an opera in seven parts'* — **'this'** refers to The Oresteia. So the answer is **opera**.

audioscript.text: By Aeschylus.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Lim composed this when she was in her mid twenties, and she also wrote the text along with Barrie Kosky.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: It's performed by six singers, a dancer, and an orchestra that, as well as standard orchestral instruments, includes electric guitar.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And a traditional Turkish stringed instrument.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Lim wrote that, because the stories in the tragedies are not easy to tell.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The sounds she creates are also disturbing, and they include breathing, sobbing, laughing, and whistling.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q35: The passage says *'The sounds she creates are also disturbing'* — Lim herself described the sounds this way. So the answer is **disturbing**.

audioscript.text: The work lasts around 75 minutes, and the rest of the concert will consist of orchestral works by the British composers Ralph Vaughan Williams.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And Frederick Delius.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Moving on now to our second concert, this will begin with instrumental music by British composers, Benjamin Britten and Judith Weir.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: After the interval, we'll go to Australia for a piece by Ross Edwards, The Tower of Remoteness, according to Edwards.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The inspiration for this piece came from nature, when he was sitting alone in the dry bed of a creek, overshadowed by the leaves of palm trees.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Listening to the birds and insects.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: The Tower of Remoteness is scored for piano and clarinet.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q36: The passage says The Tower of Remoteness *'is scored for piano and clarinet'* — **'scored for'** means it is performed by those instruments. So the answer is **clarinet**.

audioscript.text: Edwards says he realized years after writing the piece.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That he had subconsciously modeled its opening phrase on a bird call.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Ross Edwards was born in 1943 in Sydney, Australia, and studied at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music, and the universities of Adelaide and Sydney.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He's well known in Australia, and in fact, he's one of the country's most performed composers.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He's written a wide range of music, from symphonies and concertos to some composed specifically for children.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Edward's music has been described as being 'deeply connected to Australia', and it can be regarded as a Celebration of the diversity of cultures that Australia can be proud of.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q37: The passage says his music celebrates *'the diversity of cultures'* — the question asks what cultural aspect Australia celebrates. So the answer is **diversity**.

audioscript.text: The last of the three Australian composers to be represented in our festival is Carl Vine.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Born in 1954 Vine, like Liza Lim, comes from Perth, Western Australia.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: He took up the cornet at the age of five, switching to the piano five years later.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: However, he went to university to study physics before changing to composition.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q38: The passage says he *'went to university to study physics before changing to composition'* — **'composition'** here means studying music. So the answer is **physics**.

audioscript.text: After graduating, he moved to Sydney.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: And worked as a freelance pianist and composer.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: Before long, he had become prominent in Australia as a composer for dance, and in fact has written 25 scores of that type.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q39: The passage says he became prominent *'as a composer for dance'* — **'prominent'** means well known. So the answer is **dance**.

audioscript.text: In our third concert, Vine will be represented by his music for the flag handover ceremony of the Olympics held in 1996. This seven-minute orchestral piece was of course heard by millions of people worldwide.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER
audioscript.explain: Q40: The passage says his music was for *'the flag handover ceremony of the Olympics held in 1996'* — the question asks which event the music was for. So the answer is **Olympics**.

audioscript.text: And we'll hear it alongside works written by British composers, Edward Elgar, and more recently, Thomas Adès.
audioscript.speaker: SPEAKER

audioscript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: She found this was her real strength, and she studied and later taught composition, both in Australia and in other countries.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: As a composer, she has received commissions from numerous orchestras, other performers, and festivals in several countries.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Liza Lim's compositions are vibrant and full of energy, and she often explores Asian and Australian Aboriginal cultural sources.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q32: The passage says her compositions are *'vibrant and full of energy'* — **'full of'** means they show a great deal of it. So the answer is **energy**.

utterances.text: Including the native instrument the didgeridoo.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This is featured in a work called The Compass.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Her music is very expressive.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: So although it is complex, it has the power of connecting with audiences and performers alike.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q33: The passage says *'although it is complex, it has the power of connecting'* — the question says her music is expressive and also something. So the answer is **complex**.

utterances.text: In the festival, we're going to give a semi-staged performance of The Oresteia.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: This is an opera in seven parts, based on the trilogy of ancient Greek tragedies.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q34: The passage says *'This is an opera in seven parts'* — **'this'** refers to The Oresteia. So the answer is **opera**.

utterances.text: By Aeschylus.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Lim composed this when she was in her mid twenties, and she also wrote the text along with Barrie Kosky.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: It's performed by six singers, a dancer, and an orchestra that, as well as standard orchestral instruments, includes electric guitar.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And a traditional Turkish stringed instrument.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Lim wrote that, because the stories in the tragedies are not easy to tell.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The sounds she creates are also disturbing, and they include breathing, sobbing, laughing, and whistling.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q35: The passage says *'The sounds she creates are also disturbing'* — Lim herself described the sounds this way. So the answer is **disturbing**.

utterances.text: The work lasts around 75 minutes, and the rest of the concert will consist of orchestral works by the British composers Ralph Vaughan Williams.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And Frederick Delius.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Moving on now to our second concert, this will begin with instrumental music by British composers, Benjamin Britten and Judith Weir.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: After the interval, we'll go to Australia for a piece by Ross Edwards, The Tower of Remoteness, according to Edwards.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The inspiration for this piece came from nature, when he was sitting alone in the dry bed of a creek, overshadowed by the leaves of palm trees.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Listening to the birds and insects.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: The Tower of Remoteness is scored for piano and clarinet.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q36: The passage says The Tower of Remoteness *'is scored for piano and clarinet'* — **'scored for'** means it is performed by those instruments. So the answer is **clarinet**.

utterances.text: Edwards says he realized years after writing the piece.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: That he had subconsciously modeled its opening phrase on a bird call.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Ross Edwards was born in 1943 in Sydney, Australia, and studied at the Sydney Conservatorium of Music, and the universities of Adelaide and Sydney.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: He's well known in Australia, and in fact, he's one of the country's most performed composers.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: He's written a wide range of music, from symphonies and concertos to some composed specifically for children.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Edward's music has been described as being 'deeply connected to Australia', and it can be regarded as a Celebration of the diversity of cultures that Australia can be proud of.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q37: The passage says his music celebrates *'the diversity of cultures'* — the question asks what cultural aspect Australia celebrates. So the answer is **diversity**.

utterances.text: The last of the three Australian composers to be represented in our festival is Carl Vine.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Born in 1954 Vine, like Liza Lim, comes from Perth, Western Australia.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: He took up the cornet at the age of five, switching to the piano five years later.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: However, he went to university to study physics before changing to composition.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q38: The passage says he *'went to university to study physics before changing to composition'* — **'composition'** here means studying music. So the answer is **physics**.

utterances.text: After graduating, he moved to Sydney.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: And worked as a freelance pianist and composer.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: Before long, he had become prominent in Australia as a composer for dance, and in fact has written 25 scores of that type.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q39: The passage says he became prominent *'as a composer for dance'* — **'prominent'** means well known. So the answer is **dance**.

utterances.text: In our third concert, Vine will be represented by his music for the flag handover ceremony of the Olympics held in 1996. This seven-minute orchestral piece was of course heard by millions of people worldwide.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER
utterances.explain: Q40: The passage says his music was for *'the flag handover ceremony of the Olympics held in 1996'* — the question asks which event the music was for. So the answer is **Olympics**.

utterances.text: And we'll hear it alongside works written by British composers, Edward Elgar, and more recently, Thomas Adès.
utterances.speaker: SPEAKER

utterances.text: That is the end of Section 4.

audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a woman phoning a hotel about holding a party there.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you.

audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning, Clare House Hotel, Andrew speaking, I'm the Events Manager.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Andrew is the Events Manager, so Events has been written in the space.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now we shall begin.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 7.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Good morning, Clare House Hotel, Andrew speaking, I'm the Events Manager.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Good morning, Andrew.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: My name is Samantha.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: I'm arranging a party for my parents' 50th wedding anniversary.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: And I'm ringing to ask about hiring a room sometime next September, also my parents and several of the guests will need accommodation.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: OK, I'm sure we can help you with that.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Will you be having a sit down meal or a buffet?
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Probably a sit down.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: And do you know how many people there'll be?
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Around 80, I think.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Well we have two rooms that can hold that number.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: One is the Adelphi room, that can seat 85 or hold over 100 if people are standing for a buffet.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q1: The passage says the Adelphi room *'can seat 85'* — **'seat'** means the number of people who can sit down to eat. So the answer is **85**.

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: If you have live music, there's room for four or five musicians in the gallery.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Overlooking the room, our guests usually appreciate the fact that the music can be loud enough for dancing, but not too loud for conversation.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Yes, I really don't like it when you can't talk.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Exactly.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Now the Adelphi Room is at the back of the hotel, and there are French windows.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Leading out onto the terrace.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: This has a beautiful display of pots of roses at that time of the year.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q2: The passage says the terrace has *'a beautiful display of pots of roses'* — this directly tells you what is in the pots. So the answer is **roses**.

audioscript.text: Which direction does it face?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Southwest, so that side of the hotel gets the sun in the afternoon and early evening.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Very nice.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: From the terrace, you can see the area of trees within the grounds of the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q3: The passage says from the terrace *'you can see the area of trees'* — a **'group of'** trees is the same as an **'area of'** trees. So the answer is **trees**.

audioscript.text: Or you can stroll through there to the river.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: That's on the far side, so it isn't visible from the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: OK, then another option is the Carlton room.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: This is a bit bigger.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: It can hold up to 110 people, and it has the advantage of a stage, which is useful if you have any entertainment.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q4: The passage says the Carlton room *'has the advantage of a stage'* — this is a special feature it has. So the answer is **stage**.

audioscript.text: Or indeed a small band can fit onto it.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Hmm. And can you go outside from the room?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: No, the Carlton room is on the first floor.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: But on one side, the windows look out onto the lake.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Lovely.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: I think either of those rooms would be suitable.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Can I tell you about some of the options we offer in addition?
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Please do.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: As well as a meal, you can have an mc, a master of ceremonies, who'll be with you throughout the party.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: What exactly is the MC's function?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: I suppose they make a speech during the meal, if we need one, do they?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA
audioscript.explain: Q5: The passage asks if the MC will *'make a speech during the meal'* — **'give a'** speech is the same as **'make a'** speech. So the answer is **speech**.

audioscript.text: That's right.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: All our MCs are trained as public speakers, so they can easily get people's attention.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Many guests are glad to have someone who can make themselves heard above the chatter, and they're also your support.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q6: The passage says the MC is *'your support'* if anything goes wrong — **'provide'** support means they will give it to you. So the answer is **support**.

audioscript.text: If anything goes wrong, the MC will deal with it, so you can relax.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Great, I'll need to ask you about food, but something else that's important is accommodation.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: You obviously have rooms in the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: But do you also have any other accommodation, like cabins, for example?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA
audioscript.explain: Q7: The passage asks about other accommodation *'like cabins'* — this is the exact example given. So the answer is **cabins**.

audioscript.text: Yes, there are 5 in the grounds, all self contained.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: They each sleep 2 to 4 people, and have their own living room, bathroom, and small kitchen.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: That sounds perfect for what we'll need.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen and answer questions 8 to 10.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now you have various facilities, don't you?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Are they all included in the price of hiring the room?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: The pool for instance.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: Normally you'd be able to use it, but it'll be closed throughout September for refurbishment, I'm afraid.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q8: The passage says the pool *'will be closed throughout September for refurbishment'* — **'closed'** means it is **not available**. So the answer is **C**.

audioscript.text: The gym will be available though, at no extra charge.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q9: The passage says the gym *'will be available though, at no extra charge'* — **'at no extra charge'** means it is **included in the cost**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: That's open all day from 6 in the morning until midnight.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Right.
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: And the tennis courts but there is a small additional payment for those.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW
audioscript.explain: Q10: The passage says for tennis courts *'there is a small additional payment'* — **'additional payment'** means it is **available at extra charge**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: We have four courts, and it's worth booking in advance if you possibly can, as there can be quite a long waiting list for them.
audioscript.speaker: ANDREW

audioscript.text: Right, now could we discuss the food?
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: This would be dinner around 7 o'clock...
audioscript.speaker: SAMANTHA

audioscript.text: That is the end of section 1.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: You will hear a holiday company representative talking to a group of tourists in a large hotel about things they can do during their holiday.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.text: Hello, everyone.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: I'm Jake Stevens, and I'm your rep here at the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: I'm sure you'll all have a great time here.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: So, let me tell you a bit about what's on offer.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: I'll start by telling you about some of the excursions that are available for guests.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: One thing you have to do while you're here is go dolphin watching.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: On our boat trips we pretty well guarantee you'll see dolphins.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: If you don't, you can repeat the trip free of charge.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: We organize daily trips for just 35 euros.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: Unfortunately, there aren't any places left for this afternoon's trip, but come and see me to book for later in the week.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS
audioscript.explain: Q11: The passage says *'there aren't any places left for this afternoon's trip'* — **'no places left'** means it is **fully booked today**. So the answer is **G**.

audioscript.text: If you're energetic, I'd recommend our forest walk.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: It's a guided walk of about 7 km.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: There'll be a stop halfway, and you'll be provided with a drink and sandwiches.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS
audioscript.explain: Q12: The passage says *'you'll be provided with a drink and sandwiches'* — this means **food is included** in the trip. So the answer is **D**.

audioscript.text: There's some fairly steep climbs up the hills, so you need to be reasonably fit for this one.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: With good shoes, though, and bring a waterproof in case it rains.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: It's just 25 euros, all inclusive, and it's every Wednesday.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: Then on Thursdays, we organize a cycle trip, which will give you all the fun of biking without the effort.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: We'll take you and your bike up to the top of Mount Larna.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: And leave you to bike back.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: It's a 700 meter drop in just 20 kilometers, so this isn't really for inexperienced cyclists, as you'll be going pretty fast.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS
audioscript.explain: Q13: The passage says *'It's a 700 meter drop in just 20 kilometers'* — a **'drop'** means you go down, so the trip is **all downhill**. So the answer is **A**.

audioscript.text: And if it's a clear day, you'll have fantastic views.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: On our local craft tour, you can find out about the traditional activities in the island.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: And the best thing about this trip is that it's completely free.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS
audioscript.explain: Q14: The passage says *'the best thing about this trip is that it's completely free'* — **'free'** means there is **no charge**. So the answer is **E**.

audioscript.text: You'll be taken to a factory where jewelry is made, and also a ceramics center.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: If you want, you can buy some of the products, but that's entirely up to you.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: The trip starts after lunch on Thursday, and you'll return by 6:00 pm.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: If you're interested in astronomy, you may already know that the island's one of the best places in the world to observe the night sky.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: We can offer trips to the observatory on Friday for those who are interested.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: They cost €90 per person, and you'll be shown the huge telescopes, and have a talk from an expert who will explain all about how they work.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: Afterwards, we'll head down to Sunset Beach, where you can have a dip in the ocean if you want, before we head off back to the hotel.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS
audioscript.explain: Q15: The passage says *'you can have a dip in the ocean if you want'* — a **'dip'** means a short swim, so **swimming is possible**. So the answer is **F**.

audioscript.text: Finally, there's horse riding.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: This is organized by the Equestrian Center over near Playa Cortino, and it's a great experience if you're a keen horseback rider.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: Or even if you've never been on a horse before, they take you down to the beach, and you can canter along the sand and through the waves.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS
audioscript.explain: Q16: The passage says *'even if you've never been on a horse before'* — this means the trip is **suitable for beginners**. So the answer is **B**.

audioscript.text: It costs 35 euros.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: And it's available every day.
audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.
audioscript.speaker: ANNOUNCER

audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: Well, the No. 1 attraction's called 'Musical Favorites'.

audioscript.speaker: JAKE STEVENS

audioscript.text: And you'll have a chance to chat with them.
